item.title: 12 artificial reefs created in 1998 boosted local fish numbers and species richness off Miami Beach
item.description: A 2002 study examined 12 artificial reefs built off Miami Beach using limestone boulders, concrete-gravel aggregate and concrete mixed with waste tyre chips. Divers surveyed the reefs every two months from October 1998 to February 2001, recording fish species, numbers and sizes, along with spiny lobsters. They counted 97,826 fish from 146 species. The researchers found no significant difference in fish abundance, biomass or species richness between the three reef materials. However, comparisons before and after deployment showed that the artificial reefs increased local fish abundance and species richness.

item.title: Carmel River Free Project: Eastwoods’ ranch anchors $57m restoration; homes face lower flood risks
item.description: Clint Eastwood's previous artichoke farm is now being transformed into a significant wetland restoration initiative. This remarkable project aims to bolster flood protection for the surrounding communities. With the Eastwoods' generous donation, the area will see restoration of essential riparian and wetland ecosystems, fostering wildlife and promoting a more resilient river system. This change converts agricultural land into vital open space, enhancing both safety and community health.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: An Iowa priest vowed to build a shrine if he survived pneumonia; after recovering, he spent 42 years using over 100 train carloads of stone to create it
item.description: The Grotto of the Redemption in West Bend, Iowa, owes its existence to a young seminarian's promise made during his illness. Initiated by Father Dobberstein, the monumental structure took an astonishing 42 years to complete. Utilizing a variety of geological elements, over 100 train carloads of stones were involved in its construction, making it a celebrated historic landmark and one of the largest man-made grottos globally.

item.title: Five Indiana engineering students built a 12-hour wearable that helps visually impaired users detect obstacles beyond a cane or guide dog
item.description: Rose-Hulman students have developed a remarkable wearable device tailored for visually impaired individuals. This innovative headgear employs advanced sensors to identify surrounding obstacles, providing users with haptic feedback. With a remarkable twelve-hour battery life on a single charge, this device empowers users with greater independence. The project's goal is to enhance the day-to-day experiences of those with vision impairments.

item.title: In 1940, Nazis seized a painting from a Jewish collector in Vienna; 86 years later, Austria returned it to his heir in Minnesota
item.description: In a poignant gesture, an Austrian diplomat returned a stolen miniature painting to Jackie Sondell, heir to Eduard Epstein, a victim of Nazi persecution. Confiscated from Epstein's collection during his imprisonment, the artwork symbolizes Austria's acknowledgment of its historical obligations and a step towards healing. The Austrian government diligently traced Sondell and her brother to restore this cherished piece of family history.

item.title: New England is battling invasive green crabs by eating the destructive species in fancy dishes
item.description: New England's creative solution to invasive green crabs involves incorporating them into the local diet and economy. Fishermen now target these soft-shelled crabs, which are gaining popularity and higher prices. Emerging markets for green crab products, including pet snacks and whiskey infusions, aim to counteract the harmful effects of this invasive species while boosting the economy.

item.title: Former British diplomat to Pakistan is running a global marathon to help educate 25.2 million children in the country
item.description: Former diplomat Mike Nithavrianakis is undertaking marathons to raise funds for The Citizens Foundation in Pakistan, aiming to secure one million dollars to enhance educational opportunities. This crucial support is set to benefit around six thousand students for an entire academic year. Having already gathered more than $350,000, he has funded the establishment of a new campus. His drive originates from observing educational inequalities during his time in diplomacy.

item.title: Minnesota woman paid $500 for overnight shipping; box held $30,000 meant for scammers
item.description: In a remarkable turn of events, a Minnesota shipping employee's alertness prevented a scam last week. A woman, convinced she was sending $30,000 for cookbooks, exhibited signs of distress that caught the staff's attention. Authorities were called in, revealing the cash and halting its shipment. The intervention not only saved her funds but also the shipping costs, allowing her to breathe a sigh of relief.

item.title: Residential complex and possible wine press found near Sekhmet Temple at Egypt’s Memphis
item.description: An Egyptian-Chinese archaeological mission found a residential complex near Memphis's Temple of Sekhmet. Grape seeds and a limestone structure suggest a possible ancient wine press was present. Inscribed stone blocks and statue fragments also emerged from the excavation site. These findings offer insights into daily life and activities around the temple. The discoveries add significant layers to the archaeological record of ancient Memphis.

item.title: Four California seniors lose over $315,000 in crypto, gift-card and timeshare scams in just 24 hrs
item.description: Four seniors in Petaluma, California, reported separate scams within 24 hours, with suspected losses totalling more than $315,000. Police said the scams involved cryptocurrency, timeshares and gift cards. The department has warned residents to verify payment requests, ask questions and avoid acting under pressure. Police also urged people to check in on older neighbours and family members to help protect them from scams.
